title: The Cube

image.credit: collection not stated on source page; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: A dark charcoal drawing built around a cube-like form, with soft, smoky shading and deep shadows that make the shape seem to emerge from the darkness.

source.museum: collection not stated on source page
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, public-domain statement); collection not stated on the page

context: A charcoal drawing by Odilon Redon, dated 1880 on its source page, which tags it as Mysticism. Redon, a French artist, made many of his dark charcoal works, which he called his noirs, in the years around this date.

descriptions.k: This is a drawing made with black charcoal. Look for the cube. What is dark and what is light? What does it make you wonder about?
descriptions.g12: Odilon Redon drew The Cube with charcoal, a soft black stick. The drawing is full of dark, smoky shadows and a few lighter places. Where do you see light and where is it darkest? What do you imagine is hiding there?
descriptions.g35: Odilon Redon made The Cube in 1880 using only charcoal, so the picture is built from black, gray and white. Soft shading makes shapes appear and fade. The source page tags it as Mysticism. How do the dark areas create mystery, and what do you think the cube could mean?
descriptions.g68: The Cube (1880) is a charcoal drawing by the French artist Odilon Redon, who often used soft black tones to suggest dreams and the unseen. Without color, light and shadow carry all the mood. How does the shading make a simple geometric form feel strange or mysterious, and what might that tell you about Redon's aims?
descriptions.g910: Redon's The Cube (1880) shows how charcoal can move between hard form and dissolving shadow. The page tags it Mysticism, and Redon is generally linked with Symbolism, an art of mood and suggestion over direct description. How does the tonal range push a plain geometric solid toward the unfamiliar, and what do you make of that effect?
descriptions.g1112: The Cube (1880) belongs to Redon's body of charcoal drawings, which later critics tied to Symbolism and to ideas about dream, mind and the unseen. A geometric solid, normally a sign of order, here sits in a field of tone. How might this tension support more than one reading, and what limits does the work place on interpretation?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, medium (charcoal drawing), year (1880), and the page tag Mysticism read from the arthistoryproject.com page text; no concerning terms. The page labels the movement 'Surrealist', which predates the movement by decades, so the accepted label Symbolism is used instead. The collection is not stated on the page. Only page text was read; the image file was not visually inspected, and a person should confirm it (dark, moody tone; no frightening imagery) before release.

teacherNote.context: A charcoal drawing by Odilon Redon, dated 1880, a French artist known for dark, dreamlike works in charcoal. The page tags it Mysticism and does not state its collection.
directions: Have students draw a simple object in charcoal or soft pencil, then smudge the background to place it in the dark, and compare moods.
Ask students to write three different titles for the drawing and discuss how each changes what they notice.
Discuss why an artist might want a picture to feel mysterious rather than clear.
